extracted.subtask_description: Designing and running instructional activities (guided reinvention teaching experiments) to help calculus students develop formal definitions for sequence, series, and pointwise convergence. Emphasis on task design, scaffolding, graphical representations, approximation metaphors, and iterative refinement with examples/non-examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentoring program for graduate students
rubrics_metrics.description: “doing some sort of mentoring program where you match a graduate student with an older graduate student and possibly a professor so that maybe graduate students don’t feel quite so alone when they start.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentoring need not be terribly formal (e.g., assigned contact person or an older student to ask). Use mentoring to connect incoming students to departmental culture, provide vertical support, and reduce isolation during the transition to graduate school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community participation (academic and social)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Participation in the academic and social communities of the department is a critical factor in doctoral student persistence” (Herzig, 2002).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to engage both with peers (horizontal community) and faculty (vertical community). Both collaboration on assignments/discussion and socializing with peers are necessary to ease transition and support persistence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertical relationships / treatment as junior colleagues
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need the vertical sense of community established when they are treated as 'junior colleagues' by faculty members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faculty should spend time with incoming students and treat them as novice members of the practice to help them gain mathematical ability, social/cultural knowledge, and legitimate participation in research and departmental life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic expectations & departmental transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must learn the 'ins and outs' of succeeding in graduate school: realistic expectations of the nature of the degree path (sets of departmental exams to be passed, paperwork required by various campus offices, average time to graduation) and of the research process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Departments should proactively communicate concrete procedural and normative information (exam requirements, paperwork, typical timelines) to reduce confusion and help students navigate the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intro to Graduate Math / review materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestion: have some kind of 'Intro to Graduate Math' course or review manual during the summer prior to the beginning of graduate school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide preparatory coursework or review manuals to address insufficient prior knowledge. Note: student motivation to use these materials will strongly affect success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage thinking/acting/feeling like mathematicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs often expect students to master prescribed content rather than encouraging them to 'think, act, and feel as mathematicians do' (Herzig, 2004).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design coursework and opportunities that foster participation in authentic mathematical tasks (teaching, research, service) rather than focusing only on coursework mastery, to support cultural knowledge and identity formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence / Dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: Students emphasized the importance of being committed to and persevering through their degree program: 'You have to decide you’re going to do it... If you’re wishy washy, it’s over.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate student commitment and resilience; recognize perseverance as a central trait for success and persistence in graduate study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and non-defining identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Students reported that keeping life outside of mathematics helped keep them grounded: 'The one thing that I have to keep coming back to is that this doesn’t define who I am...keeping it in perspective that this is not my entire life… that’s helped a lot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to maintain outside interests and identities to reduce stress and improve learning and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate peripheral participation and identity formation
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving toward full participation involves more time, effort, broader responsibilities, and an increasing sense of identity as a master practitioner (Lave & Wenger, 1991).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide tasks and responsibilities that gradually increase students' legitimate participation (teaching, research, service) to foster identity formation as mathematicians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided reinvention instructional heuristic
rubrics_metrics.description: Design instructional activities that (a) link up with the informal situated knowledge of the students, (b) enable them to develop more sophisticated, abstract, formal knowledge, while (c) complying with the basic principle of intellectual autonomy (Gravemeijer, 1998).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guided reinvention as a design principle: start from students' informal knowledge and guide them toward formalization, while preserving student autonomy and sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with rich examples and non-examples; iterative refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin with exploration of a rich set of examples and non-examples, then move to an iterative refinement process that involves definition creation, checking examples, conflict acknowledgement, and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have students generate many examples/non-examples, propose provisional definitions, test against examples, refine definitions repeatedly. Treat each iteration as an opportunity to surface and resolve conceptual conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat conflicts between concept image and formal definition as learning opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems most commonly arise due to conflicts between the students’ concept image and their currently stated definition; experts might identify other problematic issues not recognized by students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage students to identify and resolve conflicts; use facilitator prompts to surface implicit problems. Thoughtful resolution of these issues supports stable components of students' evolving definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximation and error-analysis metaphor for limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an approximation metaphor including structures involving 'estimates,' 'error,' 'accuracy,' etc., with an unknown actual quantity, a known approximation, an associated error, and a bound on the error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame limits/ convergence in terms of approximations and bounded errors (ε as error bound, N as index after which approximations are accurate). Repeated use across contexts can make the structure of formal definitions more accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage prior reinvention (sequence → series → pointwise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students reused elements from their sequence convergence definition (N, ε, error bounds) when producing a series convergence definition, reinterpreting 'terms' as partial sums.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction so that successful reinvention in a simpler context (sequences) is explicitly mapped to more complex contexts (series, Taylor series). Prompt students to reinterpret symbols (an → Sn) and roles (terms → partial sums/approximations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graphical representations to unpack ε and N and to represent partial sums
rubrics_metrics.description: Students produced graphs of series and showed how choosing smaller ε affected the index N; they interpreted dots on a series graph as partial sums (Sn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include graphical tasks where students visualize approximations, partial sums, and ε-bands; use vertical number lines or focused x-values (for pointwise convergence) to support transition to formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facilitator prompting and session scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: Facilitators prompted students to not focus on finding formulas and guided discussion toward graphs and connections to prior definitions; the research team debriefed after each session and adjusted protocols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should use targeted prompts to redirect focus from memorizing formulas to conceptual understanding, debrief sessions and iteratively adapt tasks/protocols, and maintain a timeline of problems to track origins and resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and address common student problems during reinvention
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical problems include: (1) how to incorporate convergent sequences with 'bad [random] early behavior', (2) what is 'infinitely close?', (3) a fixed error bound allows non-examples to be included as limits?, (4) multiple uses of the 'n' notation in definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan activities and prompts that explicitly target these difficulties (e.g., emphasize existential/universal quantification, clarify 'for all ε > 0 there exists N', disambiguate notation), and give students opportunities to resolve such conflicts through example testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching-experiment structure and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: The teaching experiment comprised six 90–120 minute sessions with pair work, video transcription, content logs, debriefs, and a timeline of problems to determine origin and resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When researching or implementing reinvention tasks, structure repeated sessions, record interactions, maintain detailed logs, and use team debriefs to refine subsequent sessions and to analyze student progress.
